clinicalPearls: Chloracne is the most specific and sensitive cutaneous marker of systemic exposure to dioxins and dioxin-like halogenated aromatic hydrocarbons; its presence should trigger a search for a significant exposure.

The hallmark lesions are numerous comedones (open and closed) and small pale-yellow keratin cysts, distributed characteristically over the malar cheeks, retroauricular skin, axillae and groin rather than the usual sebaceous acne zones.
Involvement behind the ears and in the axillae/groin, sparing of the nose, and a paucity of inflammatory pustules help distinguish chloracne from acne vulgaris.
Causative agents include polychlorinated dibenzodioxins and dibenzofurans, polychlorinated biphenyls, chlorinated naphthalenes and certain chlorophenol/herbicide contaminants.

Exposure may be occupational (chemical manufacture, waste incineration, transformer work), environmental (contamination incidents) or from deliberate poisoning, and can be inhaled, ingested or absorbed through skin.
Because dioxins are highly lipophilic and slowly eliminated, chloracne can appear weeks after exposure and persist for years, sometimes fluctuating long after contact has ended.

Associated systemic effects may include hepatic dysfunction, deranged lipids, porphyria cutanea tarda, peripheral neuropathy and, with heavy exposure, an increased long-term malignancy risk, so evaluation must extend beyond the skin.
Management centres on identifying and removing the source, supportive skin care and comedo extraction; the eruption is often relatively resistant to conventional acne therapies.
reference.pathophysiology: Dioxins and dioxin-like compounds are potent ligands of the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR). On binding, the AhR translocates to the nucleus and alters transcription of genes controlling xenobiotic metabolism, cell proliferation and epidermal differentiation. In the pilosebaceous unit this drives metaplasia of sebaceous glands and follicular epithelium, with loss of sebocytes and squamous metaplasia of the sebaceous ducts, so that follicles become filled with keratin to form comedones and keratin cysts — reflected in the concept of metabolising acquired dioxin-induced skin hamartomas. The extreme lipophilicity and metabolic stability of these compounds explain their bioaccumulation in adipose tissue, prolonged half-life, delayed onset and persistence of lesions, and the potential for concurrent hepatic, porphyric, neurological and carcinogenic effects mediated through the same receptor pathway.
additionalDifferentials: oil folliculitis and coal-tar or mineral-oil acne
nevoid comedones or dilated pore lesions
milia or eruptive vellus hair cysts
additionalInvestigations: detailed occupational, environmental and exposure history including timeline
serum or adipose tissue dioxin/PCB concentrations where available
liver function tests and fasting lipid profile
urinary and plasma porphyrins to assess for porphyria cutanea tarda
skin biopsy showing comedones, keratin cysts and sebaceous gland atrophy
public-health and workplace exposure investigation to identify co-exposed individuals
redFlags: history suggesting deliberate poisoning or a mass contamination incident
hepatic dysfunction, photosensitive blistering or other features of porphyria cutanea tarda
neurological symptoms indicating systemic dioxin toxicity
widespread or rapidly progressive eruption implying heavy ongoing exposure
co-exposure of colleagues, family members or a community requiring public-health action
reference.prognosis: Chloracne is often persistent, lasting months to many years and sometimes leaving scarring, because the causative compounds are eliminated very slowly; severe cases may be resistant to treatment. The systemic outlook depends on the magnitude of exposure and any associated hepatic, neurological or malignancy risk.
pitfalls: Dismissing the eruption as ordinary acne and failing to investigate a significant toxic exposure.
Overlooking the diagnostic retroauricular, axillary and groin distribution and sparing of the nose.
Focusing only on the skin and missing hepatic, porphyric or neurological involvement.
Expecting a rapid response to standard acne therapy and underestimating persistence.
Not pursuing source identification, biological monitoring and screening of co-exposed contacts.
references: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, current edition
Adams' Occupational Skin Disease, current edition
management: Identify and remove the source of dioxin or dioxin-like exposure, since halting further exposure is the essential first step
Topical acne-directed therapy with retinoids and keratolytics, and oral retinoids such as isotretinoin for extensive comedonal and cystic disease
Comedone extraction and management of keratin cysts, with scar management for residual disease
Monitor and manage systemic toxicity, including liver function and lipids, screening for porphyria cutanea tarda and assessing for peripheral neuropathy
Occupational and public health investigation to define the exposure and protect others
Multidisciplinary input across dermatology and occupational medicine
Long-term follow-up given the delayed onset and persistence of lesions over months to years
